cards.explanation: The answer is that no house for the LORD's Name had been built yet. That's the reason the text gives. The people were still sacrificing on the high places "…because a house for the Name of the LORD had not yet been built." Solomon, David's son and Israel's king, was still busy building that house, along with his palace and the wall (1 Kings 3:1). Anybody who has waited on a building project knows the feeling.

The answer is True. The text says it straight out: "…Solomon loved the LORD and walked in the statutes of his father David…" (1 Kings 3:3). The writer puts that right up front. Then comes a little "except," and we'll get to that. The love is real, and the text says so first.

The answer is incense. The verse says Solomon walked in his father's statutes, "…except that he sacrificed and burned incense on the high places." (1 Kings 3:3). So the sacrificing and the incense both happened there. Incense is the word in the verse, friends.

The answer is "Ask, and I will give it to you!" In the dream at Gibeon, that's what God says (1 Kings 3:5). That's an open door for Solomon, Israel's king. I think I'd have stood there with my mouth open for a full minute. What a way to start a dream.

The answer is that David walked before Him faithfully. Solomon says God showed his father David loving devotion "…because he walked before You in faithfulness, righteousness, and uprightness of heart." (1 Kings 3:6). Notice Solomon honors his dad before he asks for a single thing. That's a good way to start a conversation with God.

The answer is child. Solomon says, "But I am only a little child, not knowing how to go out or come in." (1 Kings 3:7). Here is a king saying he doesn't know how to do the job. I think that kind of honesty takes some nerve.

The answer is True. Solomon says he's among the people God chose, "…a people too numerous to count or number." (1 Kings 3:8). That's a lot of people for one king to lead. Count them? Friends, I can't even count the crumbs on my counter.

The answer is a heart to judge with understanding. Solomon asks, "Therefore give Your servant an understanding heart to judge Your people and to discern between good and evil." (1 Kings 3:9). God said ask, and Solomon asked for help doing the job. I think that's one of the best requests ever made.

The answer is False. Solomon doesn't say anyone refuses to obey. He asks, "For who is able to govern this great people of Yours?" (1 Kings 3:9). His need comes from the size of the people and the weight of the job. That's all the text gives.

The answer is True. God says, "…I will do what you have asked." (1 Kings 3:12). The text says it pleased the Lord that Solomon made this request (1 Kings 3:10). The answer is a plain yes. No fine print, friends.

The answer is wise. God says, "I will give you a wise and discerning heart…" (1 Kings 3:12). Wise and discerning, the very thing Solomon asked for. It's a gift to Solomon, the king, and it's a big one.
The answer is False. God says, "…so that there will never have been another like you, nor will there ever be." (1 Kings 3:12). Nobody before, nobody after. That is some serious wisdom, friends.

The answer is riches and honor. God says He'll give Solomon what he did not request, "…both riches and honor…" (1 Kings 3:13). Solomon asked for wisdom, and God promises riches and honor too. I think that's the best kind of surprise.

The answer is prolong. God says, "So if you walk in My ways and keep My statutes and commandments, just as your father David did, I will prolong your days." (1 Kings 3:14). Notice the "if." The promise is tied to walking in God's ways, the way David did.

The answer is that he holds a feast for them. After the offerings, the text says, "Then he held a feast for all his servants." (1 Kings 3:15). Solomon wakes from the dream, goes before the ark, and then throws a feast. I'd show up early for that one, friends.
